stories.title: The Prophecy of the Afghan Mystic
stories.story:
## The Prophecy of the Afghan Mystic

*No chronicle records a mystic's prophecy at Najibabad; the tale is local tradition, set here against the documented founding of the town and its fort.*

Najibabad takes its name from **Najib-ud-Daulah**, a Yusufzai Afghan who came to Rohilkhand as a soldier of fortune and rose in the service of the Rohilla chief **Ali Muhammad Khan**. In the mid-eighteenth century he founded the town at the foot of the Siwalik hills, close to the crossings of the Ganga, and around **1755** raised the stone fort known locally as **Pathargarh**.

Tradition says that before the walls went up, a wandering Afghan fakir blessed the site but warned that it would rise high and fall soon. No Persian history of the period mentions him. The shape of the tale, though, follows what really happened. Najib became one of the most powerful men in India: **Ahmad Shah Abdali** left him in charge at Delhi in **1757**, and he was a key ally of the Afghans at **Panipat in 1761**. Yet within two years of his death in **1770**, Pathargarh had been taken and his family scattered. Later generations, looking back, may simply have placed the warning in a holy man's mouth.

stories.title: The Betrayal of the Trusted General
stories.story:
## The Betrayal of the Trusted General

*The "trusted general" of popular retellings appears in no record; what history documents is the fall of Pathargarh to the Marathas in 1772.*

After Najib-ud-Daulah died in 1770, his son **Zabita Khan** inherited his lands and his enemies. The Marathas had not forgotten Panipat, nor Najib's part in bringing Abdali into India. In **1772** Maratha commanders, among them **Mahadji Scindia**, moved into Zabita Khan's country together with the forces of the emperor **Shah Alam II**, who had just returned to Delhi under Maratha protection. Zabita Khan was beaten near the Ganga crossings and fled, and Pathargarh, which sheltered his family and treasure, fell soon after.

Popular retellings explain the swift fall through a treacherous commander who opened the gates. No such figure is named in the Persian or Maratha sources. The version that blames the British is also out of place: the East India Company's **Rohilla War of 1774** was fought, alongside the Nawab of Awadh, against **Hafiz Rahmat Khan** of Bareilly, not at Najibabad.

The real story was harsh enough. Contemporary accounts say the victors carried off Zabita Khan's women and children, and later writers report that Najib's tomb was damaged, a humiliation his family did not forget.

stories.title: The Hidden Treasure of the Rohilla Chiefs
stories.story:
## The Hidden Treasure of the Rohilla Chiefs

*Treasure tales cling to every ruined fort; the documented core here is the plunder of Pathargarh in 1772 and, much later, outlaw legends of the 1920s.*

The idea of a Rohilla hoard is not baseless. Najib-ud-Daulah controlled rich lands in the upper Doab and Rohilkhand and, as the dominant power at Delhi, handled imperial revenues. Pathargarh was his family's strongbox. When it fell in 1772, accounts describe a large haul of cash, jewels, guns and goods carried off by the victors, so large that its division caused bitter quarrels between the Maratha leaders and the emperor.

Local storytellers prefer to believe that not everything was found. They speak of a sealed chamber under the palace floors, guarded by traps or by a curse. No such chamber has ever been documented, and the fort's interior buildings have long since been stripped away.

A second layer of legend belongs to the twentieth century. The bandit **Sultana Daku**, active in the forests of the Bijnor and Najibabad area until his capture and execution in **1924**, is said in local lore to have used Pathargarh as a hideout and buried loot there. That too remains rumour. The visible treasure is the fort's stone itself.

stories.title: The Phantom Army of Rohilla Warriors
stories.story:
## The Phantom Army of Rohilla Warriors

*The ghostly army is modern folklore; the history behind it is the short, violent arc of Najib's line, ending with Ghulam Qadir in 1788–89.*

People living near Pathargarh tell of hoofbeats at night, of turbaned figures on the ramparts, and of a mounted chief surveying the walls. No one has documented such sightings, and stories of this kind gather around many ruins in north India. What they preserve is the memory of a fighting household.

Zabita Khan recovered his position after 1772 and played a part in Mughal politics at Delhi until his death in **1785**. His son **Ghulam Qadir**, who as a boy is said to have been among those taken at Pathargarh, became the most notorious of the line. In **1788** he seized Delhi, deposed and blinded the aged emperor **Shah Alam II**, and ransacked the palace in search of hidden wealth. Mahadji Scindia's forces caught him, and he was put to death in **1789**.

With him the independent power of Najib's house ended. The phantom horsemen of local lore can be read as the afterimage of those few decades, when soldiers from a small Siwalik town rode all the way to the Red Fort.

stories.title: The Curse of the Deserted Village
stories.story:
## The Curse of the Deserted Village

*No record names a village destroyed for the fort or a Sufi who cursed it; this tale is local tradition, set here against what is known of the town's later history.*

The legend tells of a village cleared to make way for the fort and of a holy man who cursed the new stronghold to know only brief glory. Neither the village nor the saint appears in surviving records, and historians treat the story as a way of explaining the fort's rapid decline after the fact.

The decline itself is well documented. After 1789 the region passed through Maratha and Awadh hands, and in **1801** the Nawab of Awadh ceded Rohilkhand, including the Najibabad country, to the East India Company. Najib's descendants kept estates and the title of Nawab, but no sovereignty.

The last flare came in **1857**. **Mahmud Khan**, Nawab of Najibabad and a descendant of Najib-ud-Daulah, took control of Bijnor district when Company rule collapsed in the region and held it for several months, until British forces returned in 1858. His defeat brought confiscation, and Pathargarh was left to decay.

Today the fort survives only in fragments, and the curse story is local memory's explanation for so swift a fall.

stories.title: The Love Story of Maharaja and Maharani Gayatri Devi
stories.story:
## The Love Story of Maharaja and Maharani Gayatri Devi

*Drawn from Gayatri Devi's memoir A Princess Remembers (1976) and published biographies; claims that the palace was redesigned for her are later embellishment.*

**Sawai Man Singh II** of Jaipur first met **Gayatri Devi**, a princess of **Cooch Behar**, in **1931**, when he came to Calcutta to play polo. She was about twelve; he was nineteen, already married, and a celebrated player. In her memoir she recalls being dazzled by the dashing sportsman, and as she grew up, through meetings in India and England, the friendship turned to love. Her mother, Maharani **Indira Devi**, was cautious: Jaipur already had two maharanis, and Gayatri Devi would be the third. After a long courtship they married in **1940**.

Rambagh became the couple's home. The building had begun in **1835** as a garden house, later served as a royal hunting lodge, and Man Singh had made it his principal residence in the **1920s**, years before their courtship. The tale that its gardens and corridors were built for her is therefore a romantic invention. What is true is that she made it her own, filling it with guests, horses and the bustle of the polo season.

Their partnership outlasted the princely order. Man Singh served as **Rajpramukh** of Rajasthan from 1949, and in **1957** Rambagh was turned into a hotel. Gayatri Devi entered politics and won a Lok Sabha seat in **1962** with a record majority. Man Singh died after collapsing during a polo match in England in **1970**; she lived on until **2009**.

stories.title: The Peacock Garden Miracle
stories.story:
## The Peacock Garden Miracle

*The story of a hermit who summoned the peacocks is folklore; the peafowl themselves are a natural part of Jaipur's gardens.*

Rambagh stands in some forty-seven acres of Mughal-style gardens, with lawns, water channels and fountains laid out around the palace. Its most famous residents are its **peacocks**, which strut across the lawns and call from the rooftops at dusk.

A popular story says that a hermit from the **Aravalli** hills told Man Singh II the palace would prosper only if it became a refuge for peacocks, and that birds flocked from across Rajasthan once the garden was ready. Nothing in the palace's history supports this, and no such birds needed summoning. The **Indian peafowl** is common around Jaipur, thriving in gardens, temple groves and farmland, where local custom protects it. Hindu tradition links the peacock to **Krishna**, whose crown bears its feather, and to the war god **Kartikeya**, who rides one; killing a peacock has long been taboo in Rajasthan. In **1963** it was declared India's national bird.

What the legend captures is real enough: a large walled garden with water and shade, in a semi-arid city, becomes a natural haven, and generations of Rambagh's gardeners have kept it so. Guests still wake to the cries of the birds, and the peacock recurs in the palace's décor, a motif shared with Jaipur's **City Palace**, whose Peacock Gate is among its best-known features.

stories.title: The Ghost of the Loyal Servant
stories.story:
## The Ghost of the Loyal Servant

*The ghostly servant is hotel lore without documentary basis; the palace's traditional origin as a house for a royal attendant is widely recorded.*

Rambagh's own beginnings are tied to a servant. In **1835**, in the reign of the infant Maharaja **Ram Singh II**, a small garden house was built here, traditionally said to be for **Kesar Badaran**, a favoured attendant of the young ruler's household. Ram Singh later used it as a hunting lodge, and his successor **Madho Singh II** enlarged it, with work often credited to the engineer **Samuel Swinton Jacob**.

Staff and guests sometimes speak of a figure with a lantern seen in the corridors before dawn, an old retainer still making his rounds. The story is told without names or dates, and there is no record of a particular servant to attach it to. It belongs to a familiar genre of palace-hotel tales.

Yet it reflects something true about the place. Princely households ran on large staffs of bearers, cooks, grooms, gardeners and guards, many of whom served one family for decades, son following father. When Rambagh became a hotel in **1957**, and later came under the **Taj** group in 1972, a number of old retainers and their families went on working there. Their knowledge of the building, its routines and its ceremonies carried the life of the royal house into the hotel era. In that sense the lantern-bearer of the story stands for a real and largely unrecorded community whose labour kept the palace running.

stories.title: The Royal Wedding Miracle
stories.story:
## The Royal Wedding Miracle

*The storm-and-puja story is popular lore; the wedding itself is well recorded, including the fact that it took place in Cooch Behar, not at Rambagh.*

Sawai Man Singh II married Gayatri Devi on **9 May 1940**. The ceremony was held at **Cooch Behar**, the bride's home in north Bengal, as custom required, with the groom's party travelling across India for it. By princely standards it was a restrained affair: Europe was at war, and the match had needed long persuasion on both sides.

A story told in Jaipur says that a sudden storm threatened the celebrations at Rambagh until the royal priest performed a puja and the clouds parted. Since the wedding took place far away in Bengal, the tale is at best a confusion with festivities after the couple reached Jaipur, and no record describes such a storm.

The genuine drama lay elsewhere. Arriving in Jaipur, the new Maharani found a court where royal women still kept **purdah** and lived in the zenana. Her memoir describes her frustration with these restrictions and her pleasure in Rambagh, where life was freer, with riding, tennis and guests. In **1943** she founded the **Maharani Gayatri Devi Girls' Public School**, encouraging Jaipur's girls toward education and, gradually, out of seclusion. That reform, rather than any weather miracle, is the lasting mark the marriage left on the city.

stories.title: The Famine Relief Palace
stories.story: During the severe drought of 1920s, Maharaja Umaid Singh commissioned this palace as a famine relief project. The construction provided employment to over 3,000 people for 15 years, saving the population from starvation. The palace became a symbol of royal benevolence and far-sighted governance.

stories.title: The Curse of the Sacred Grove
stories.story: The palace was built on the site of a sacred grove dedicated to a local deity. According to legend, the royal priest warned that disturbing the sacred site would bring misfortune. To appease the deity, a special temple was built within the palace complex, and daily rituals are still performed there.

stories.title: The Hidden Treasury
stories.story: Local legends speak of a hidden treasury within the palace containing the accumulated wealth of centuries of Marwar rulers. The treasure is said to be protected by ancient curses and can only be found by those pure of heart. Many have searched, but none have succeeded in locating this legendary wealth.

stories.title: The British Architect's Secret
stories.story: The British architect Henry Vaughan Lanchester, who designed the palace, is said to have incorporated secret passages and hidden chambers unknown to the royal family. These hidden spaces were supposedly used by British intelligence during the independence movement. Some of these passages are still being discovered today.

stories.title: The Royal Flag Mystery
stories.story: The palace flag is raised every morning and lowered at sunset, following royal tradition. Legend says that if the flag ever remains flying at night, it signifies the end of the royal lineage. In 1947, during independence, the flag accidentally remained up all night, leading to predictions of the monarchy's end.

stories.title: The Floating Palace
stories.story: The palace was designed to appear as if floating on water during the monsoon season. Maharaja Suraj Mal created an elaborate system of canals and water chambers that could flood the lower levels, making the palace seem like it was rising from a lake. This architectural marvel amazed visitors from across India.

stories.title: The 900 Fountains of Suraj Bhawan
stories.story: Suraj Bhawan contains 900 fountains that could create spectacular water displays. According to legend, each fountain represented a victory of Maharaja Suraj Mal. The hydraulic system was so advanced that it could simulate different types of rainfall, from gentle showers to thunderous downpours, entertaining royal guests.

stories.title: The Hidden Water Tunnels
stories.story: Beneath the palace lies a network of hidden water tunnels used for both irrigation and defense. Local stories tell of secret escape routes that allowed the royal family to flee during attacks. These tunnels connected to distant water bodies and could flood enemy positions during sieges.

stories.title: The Monsoon Festival Miracle
stories.story: Every year during the monsoon, the palace hosts the Kajli Teej festival. Legend says that on this day, the palace's water systems activate automatically, creating artificial rain even during drought years. The synchronized fountain displays are said to represent the cosmic dance of Lord Krishna.

stories.title: The Curse of the Flooded Garden
stories.story: The palace's famous gardens were once cursed by a court poet who was unjustly punished. He predicted that the gardens would flood every monsoon, destroying the carefully manicured landscapes. Strangely, certain sections of the garden do flood annually, despite modern drainage systems.

stories.title: The Victory Palace
stories.story: Raja Bakhtawar Singh built this palace to commemorate his victory over the Marathas in 1793. The foundation stone was laid with the blood of enemy commanders mixed with mortar, symbolizing the triumph of Rajput valor. The palace's main gate still bears the marks of this historic victory.

stories.title: The Hidden Treasury of Alwar
stories.story: Legend speaks of a vast treasury hidden beneath the palace containing the wealth accumulated by 34 generations of Alwar rulers. The treasure is protected by multiple layers of secret chambers and deadly traps. Only the rightful heir with pure Rajput blood can allegedly access this ancestral wealth.

stories.title: The Curse of the Poet-King
stories.story: Raja Bakhtawar Singh, a patron of arts, once punished a court poet for treason. The poet cursed that the palace would never know lasting peace. Historical records show that the palace witnessed numerous conflicts, including internal family feuds and external invasions, lending credence to this legend.

stories.title: The British Resident's Secret
stories.story: During British rule, the palace hosted several British residents. One resident supposedly discovered a secret chamber containing documents that could have changed the course of Indian history. He mysteriously disappeared while trying to smuggle these documents to Calcutta, and his ghost is said to haunt the palace corridors.
